Pretraining gives a transformer a general model of language, but it does not teach it a task.
adapts a pretrained model to a task with labeled examples: it adds a small task-specific layer, the

, and continues training. Because the pretrained layers already encode most of what the task needs, a few thousand labeled examples are often enough where training from scratch would need millions. This section describes the heads for the most common tasks, the choice between freezing and training the pretrained layers, the hyperparameters that matter, parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA, and a complete fine-tuning loop.

A DistilBERT model fine-tuned on the SQuAD question-answering dataset receives the question “When was the University of Basel founded?” and the passage “The University of Basel was founded in 1460 and is the oldest university in Switzerland. Its faculty of science offers a master program in computer science.” The tokenizer turns both into 40 tokens; the year becomes the two sub-word tokens
. The answer is “1460”. For the question “Which country is the university in?”, the same model extracts “switzerland” from the same passage.

How much of the pretrained model should change? Three strategies trade cost against accuracy.
encoder keeps all pretrained weights and trains the head alone. This is the linear probe of

: it is fast, it needs few examples, and one encoder can serve many tasks at once, since the embeddings can be computed once and reused. Its accuracy is limited by how much of the task the pretrained representation already captures.

trains all weights together with the head. It reaches the best accuracy, because the representation itself adapts to the task, but it needs more labeled data and computation, and it produces a complete copy of the model for every task. With too much training, the model can also lose general abilities it had before, an effect called

trains only the top layers and freezes the lower ones, which hold the most general features. It sits between the two in cost and accuracy.

A few pitfalls are common. Small datasets make fine-tuning unstable: two runs with different random seeds can differ by several percentage points, so results should be averaged over several seeds and compared on a validation set (

). The model overfits within a few epochs, so the validation loss decides when to stop. Inputs longer than the maximum length are truncated, which may cut off the part that decides the label. And a text classifier trained on one kind of text, such as tweets, may transfer poorly to another, such as product reviews.

Since every task only needs its own small pair of matrices, one base model can serve many tasks, with the matching adapter loaded per request.

goes one step further: it stores the frozen base model in 4-bit numbers and trains LoRA adapters on top, which fits the fine-tuning of a 65-billion-parameter model onto a single graphics processor with 48 GB of memory.
The following loop fine-tunes a small pretrained encoder for binary classification with the Hugging Face
loads the pretrained encoder and adds a new, randomly initialized classification head; the model computes the cross-entropy loss itself when it receives the labels.

import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification

name = "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"          # 22.7M parameters
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name, num_labels=2)

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=5e-5, weight_decay=0.01)
model.train()
for texts, labels in train_batches:                       # mini-batches of 32 examples
    enc = tokenizer(texts, padding=True, truncation=True,
                    max_length=64, return_tensors="pt")
    loss = model(**enc, labels=torch.tensor(labels)).loss  # cross-entropy
    loss.backward()                                       # backpropagation
    optimizer.step()
    optimizer.zero_grad()

Fine-tuning changes how a model behaves: the labels it assigns, the format and style of its outputs, the tasks it can perform. It is a poor way to give a model new facts. Facts learned into the weights cannot be updated without training again, cannot be cited, and mix with what the model already believed. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies facts at query time instead, as
discusses: fine-tune for behavior, retrieve for knowledge.
